title: Cholera Breaks Out of Bengal
text: In 1817 a particularly virulent outbreak of cholera struck Bengal. Known as 'Asiatic cholera', it began in Jessore near Calcutta, appeared throughout India, and then spread into the Far East and as far as Muscat, Tehran and Baghdad. This first cholera pandemic finally reached the Mediterranean in 1823 and died down.

source.name: PMC (Archives of Iranian Medicine): History of Cholera Outbreaks in Iran during the 19th and 20th Centuries

source2.name: US National Library of Medicine: Cholera Online, 1817-1923

title: Jung Bahadur Seizes Nepal
text: In 1846 Jung Bahadur took control of Nepal's government after killing Gagan Singh, who had plotted with the junior queen. He later exiled the king and queen, became prime minister for life and took the hereditary title Rana. His family held the office, passed from brother to brother, until 1951, while the Shah kings were left with an honorary role.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Jung Bahadur

title: A College for Canal Builders
text: In 1847 the Roorkee College of Civil Engineering opened, mainly to train Indian engineers for the ongoing Ganges Canal. It was later renamed Thomason College after its founder, James Thomason. It became the University of Roorkee in 1949, and in 2001 it was declared India's seventh Indian Institute of Technology, today's IIT Roorkee.

source.name: IIT Roorkee: About Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee

title: A Boy King Loses the Mountain of Light
text: Duleep Singh, born in Lahore and declared Maharaja of the Punjab at just 5, was still only 10 when the East India Company took control after two Anglo-Sikh wars. With the annexation of the Punjab in 1849, he was forced to give up his lands and the Koh-i-noor, the 'mountain of light' diamond, which joined Queen Victoria's crown jewels.

source.name: Historic Royal Palaces: Duleep Singh, the Last Sikh Maharaja

title: Peasants Say No to Indigo
text: In 1859 farmers in Jessore and Nadia, the two major indigo-growing districts, joined together to free themselves from the planters who forced them to grow the crop. They used social boycotts, non-cooperation and sometimes armed revolt. Dinabandhu Mitra's 1860 play Nildarpan, 'Mirror of Indigo', won them public support, and a new law then banned forcing farmers to grow indigo.

source.name: Banglapedia: Indigo Resistance Movement

title: Dreaming of a Muslim Cambridge
text: On a visit to England in 1869-70, the scholar Sayyid Ahmad Khan drew up plans for 'a Muslim Cambridge'. In May 1875 a Muslim school opened at Aligarh, and after retiring he devoted himself to turning it into a college, whose foundation stone the viceroy laid in January 1877. Despite conservative opposition, the college made rapid progress.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Sir Sayyid Ahmad Khan

title: A Queen Proclaimed Empress
place: About four miles north-west of Delhi, India
text: On January 1, 1877, the Viceroy Lord Lytton staged an Imperial Assemblage outside Delhi to announce Queen Victoria's new title, Empress of India. Sixty-three princes attended, and about 100,000 people camped nearby with horses, elephants and camels. The painter Valentine Prinsep later spent months travelling India for sittings, squeezing nearly 160 recognisable portraits into one enormous canvas.

source.name: Royal Collection Trust: The Imperial Assemblage held at Delhi, 1 January 1877

title: A Party Born in Dhaka
text: On December 30, 1906, an All India Muslim Education Conference held at Shahbag in Dhaka gave birth to the Muslim League. Nawab Salimullah proposed creating a political platform, and the conference chairman, Nawab Viqar-ul-Mulk, supported his motion. Salimullah backed the recent Partition of Bengal and wanted a party to counter the agitation against it.

source.name: Banglapedia: Muslim League

title: Bhagat Singh's Last Day
text: Bhagat Singh popularised the cry 'Inquilab zindabad', 'Long live the revolution'. After a British police officer, J.P. Saunders, was killed by mistake and bombs were thrown in Delhi's Central Legislative Assembly, he was tried and led a prison hunger strike. On March 23, 1931, aged 23, he was hanged in Lahore with Rajguru and Sukhdev Thapar; he spent that day reading about Lenin.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Bhagat Singh

title: The Lahore Resolution
text: In March 1940 Muhammad Ali Jinnah called a general session of the All India Muslim League in Lahore. On March 23 Fazlul Huq moved a resolution that Muslim-majority areas in the north-western and eastern zones should form 'independent states', and it was adopted the next day. In 1946 the word 'states' was changed to the singular 'state'.

source.name: Banglapedia: Lahore Resolution

title: India Belongs Only to Me
text: 'Europe belongs to Picasso, Matisse, Braque, and many others. India belongs only to me,' wrote the painter Amrita Sher-Gil, who blended Ajanta cave painting with Paris-trained oil technique. In 1941 she moved to Lahore and was preparing her first solo show there when she fell ill and died on December 5. Her last unfinished works moved towards abstraction.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Amrita Sher-Gil

title: The Famine of Fifty
place: Undivided Bengal (today's Bangladesh and West Bengal, India)
text: Bengalis call the 1943 famine panchaxer manvantar, 'the famine of fifty', after the Bengali year 1350. Rice imports from Burma had stopped, and a wartime 'denial' policy withdrew boats from coastal districts. Rice that sold for under 6 rupees a maund in Calcutta in early 1942 reached over 100 in some districts, and between 3.5 and 3.8 million people died.

source.name: Banglapedia: Famine, 1943

title: The First Asian Games
text: In 1951 New Delhi hosted the very first Asian Games. Athletes from 11 nations competed in six sports: football, athletics, basketball, cycling, swimming and weightlifting. From 1954 the Games were held every four years, and by the 2002 Games in Pusan, South Korea, 41 nations took part in events across 38 sports.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Asian Games

title: Sharing Six Rivers
text: In 1960, after nine years of negotiations, India and Pakistan signed the Indus Waters Treaty, with the World Bank also signing. The western rivers, the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab, went to Pakistan, and the eastern Ravi, Beas and Sutlej to India. US President Dwight Eisenhower called it one bright spot in a depressing world picture, and it has survived frequent tensions.

source.name: World Bank: Fact Sheet, The Indus Waters Treaty 1960 and the Role of the World Bank

title: Sugar, Salt and Water
text: In 1968 doctors at the Cholera Research Laboratory hospital in Dhaka, including David Nalin, Richard Cash, Rafiqul Islam and Majid Molla, showed that a simple oral glucose-sodium drink could keep cholera patients' body salts in balance. It cut the need for intravenous fluids by 80 per cent. The Lancet later called oral rehydration therapy the most important medical advance of the 20th century.

source.name: PMC: Development of oral rehydration salt solution, a triumph of medical science

title: The Great Cyclone of 1970
text: On November 12-13, 1970, the deadliest cyclone in Bangladesh's history struck the coast, with winds of about 222 km/h and a storm surge up to about 10.6 metres. It hit places such as Char Tazumuddin, Patuakhali and Barguna, and battered Chittagong. The official death toll was 500,000 and may have been higher, including some 46,000 inland fishermen.

source.name: Banglapedia: Cyclone

title: Chipko Saves the Ash Trees
place: Mandal, near Gopeshwar, Chamoli, Uttarakhand, India
text: On April 24, 1973, villagers of Mandal near Gopeshwar, led by Chandi Prasad Bhatt and the Dasholi Gram Swarajya Mandal, stopped contractors for a sports goods company from felling 14 ash trees. This was the birth of the Chipko movement. In December they stopped the same company's agents again in the Phata-Rampur forests.

source.name: India Environment Portal (Centre for Science and Environment): Landmarks on the Chipko trail

title: Loans Without Collateral
text: In 1976 Muhammad Yunus, an economics professor at the University of Chittagong, began an experiment in Jobra village: giving collateral-free credit to landless people. The rural banking project became Grameen Bank, a specialised bank set up in October 1983 and owned mostly by its borrowers, most of them poor women. In 2006 Yunus and the bank jointly won the Nobel Peace Prize.

source.name: Banglapedia: Grameen Bank

title: Pasang Lhamu Reaches the Top
text: On April 22, 1993, Pasang Lhamu Sherpa reached the summit of Everest by the South Col route, after attempts in 1990, 1991 and 1992. Her expedition had been organised to put the first Nepalese woman on top of the world. She died after an unprepared bivouac at the South Summit on the way down, and was honoured with the Star of Nepal.

source.name: American Alpine Journal: Asia, Nepal, Everest, First Ascent by a Nepalese Woman and Tragedy

title: Bhutan Switches On Television
text: Bhutan got its own national television on June 2, 1999, timed to celebrate the Silver Jubilee of the Fourth King's enthronement. Queen Mother Tseyring Pem Wangchuck switched on the Bhutan Broadcasting Service at Sangaygang, and broadcasts ran for just three hours a day. It all began in 1973, when volunteers went on air with a makeshift radio studio for half an hour every Sunday.

source.name: Bhutan Broadcasting Service: BBS, a journey through time, from radio pioneers to high-definition TV

title: The Kashmir Earthquake
text: On October 8, 2005, a magnitude 7.6 earthquake shook northern Pakistan and Kashmir. At least 86,000 people were killed in Pakistan and another 1,350 in India, and an estimated 4 million were left homeless. The worst damage was around Muzaffarabad, the town of Uri lost 80 percent of its buildings, and buildings collapsed as far away as Lahore.

source.name: USGS: Today in Earthquake History, October 8

title: A Schoolgirl's Secret Diary
text: From January 3, 2009, the BBC published for ten weeks the diary of an 11-year-old in Swat, under the pen name Gul Makai, a heroine of a Pakhtun folktale. The writer was Malala Yousafzai. After the Taliban outlawed girls' education in the valley, a BBC Urdu journalist phoned her for 30 minutes every day to hear about her life.

source.name: The Express Tribune: Where it all started, 'A diary that highlighted Swat's human tragedy'
